title: Cystic Glioblastoma: A Mimicker of Infection? A Case Report and Literature Review
case_prompt:
A 40-year-old Haitian man presented with a two-week history of progressive right-sided weakness, dysesthesias, and headaches. He denied dizziness, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, or neck stiffness. On neurological examination, he had upper motor neuron–pattern weakness (4/5) in the right upper and lower extremities, increased temperature sensitivity on the right side, and right lower-extremity gait abnormality; reflexes were intact and cranial nerves were normal.

A noncontrast CT scan of the head revealed widespread cystic lesions throughout the cerebral hemispheres. Brain MRI demonstrated numerous bilateral intraparenchymal cystic enhancing lesions, some with internal hemorrhagic components. The largest was a 5.0 × 3.4 × 4.0 cm cyst in the left frontoparietal region causing mass effect, with additional lesions in the left caudate head, left basal ganglia rimmed with hemorrhage, and the right superior frontal white matter. There was a 5 mm rightward septal shift.

CT of the chest and abdomen showed no primary or metastatic masses. Syphilis serology was nonreactive, and the Quantiferon TB test was reactive; the patient had no prior treatment for latent tuberculosis. CSF analysis revealed 10 WBC/mm3, protein 69 g/L, glucose 70 mmol/L, and cytology showing atypical cells. Other infectious studies—including VDRL, routine blood cultures, AFB smear, serum Cryptococcus antigen, HIV, galactomannan, Fungitell, and toxoplasmosis serology—were negative.

Three days after admission, his right lower-extremity weakness progressed to paralysis, and repeat CT of the head showed hyperdense material layering within a cystic lesion, suggestive of intracystic hemorrhage. He was started on dexamethasone for vasogenic edema, with slight improvement. Despite negative cysticercosis serology, he received empiric albendazole, praziquantel, and levetiracetam. Given the reactive Quantiferon test, he was also treated for latent tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurocysticercosis was considered because of the cystic lesions and epidemiology—“Despite cysticercosis antibodies being tested negative, the patient was also initiated on albendazole, praziquantel, and levetiracetam for the empiric treatment of neurocysticercosis and seizure prophylaxis.”  
2. Brain tuberculoma was suspected due to a positive Quantiferon and lack of prior therapy—“Syphilis serology was nonreactive, and the Quantiferon test was reactive... Due to high suspicion of brain tuberculoma, the patient was treated for latent tuberculosis.”  
3. Metastatic disease was ruled out by systemic imaging—“CT chest and abdomen did not show any primary or metastatic masses.”  
4. Bacterial and other fungal or parasitic abscesses were excluded by negative cultures and serologies—“Other infectious workup including venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL), routine blood cultures, acid-fast bacillus (AFB), and serum Cryptococcus antigen was negative.”  
5. Primary central nervous system neoplasm was suspected when CSF cytology showed atypical cells—“CSF cytology was significant for atypical cells, raising concern for malignancy.”
